The hogfish Lachnolaimus maximus is a large, sexually dimorphic labrid that inhabits reef and seagrass habitats throughout the western Atlantic. Adult males are capable of reaching an ultimate total length of 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], a size that distinguishes them as one of the larger members of the family Labridae within their range. This maximum size is attained gradually over many years, with growth rates that slow considerably after the onset of sexual maturation. The species is known to exhibit protogynous hermaphroditism, with all individuals initially functioning as females before transitioning to males later in life. Field surveys conducted across the Florida Keys and Gulf of Mexico have provided extensive morphometric data for this economically important species, which is targeted by both commercial and recreational fisheries. The length-weight relationship derived from these populations follows the general labrid pattern, allowing reliable estimation of body mass from total length. These measurements are particularly useful for fisheries management, as they permit rapid assessment of condition and reproductive status of captured individuals without the need for direct weighing in the field.

The onset of reproductive capability in hogfish occurs at a relatively modest body size, with individuals reaching puberty at a total length of 18.1 centimeters [Lp = 18.1 centimeters]. This threshold corresponds to the size at which the gonads first begin to develop and the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes fully activated. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 112.3 grams [Wwp = 112.3 grams], a value calculated from the species-specific length-weight relationship that reflects the allometric scaling of mass with length. This pubertal size is reached within the first few years of life, depending on local environmental conditions and food availability. The relatively small size at puberty compared to the ultimate length indicates that individuals become reproductively competent while still having considerable somatic growth ahead of them, a pattern common among iteroparous fishes that spawn repeatedly across multiple seasons. This early maturation strategy likely enhances overall lifetime reproductive output by allowing individuals to participate in several spawning seasons before reaching senescence.

Reproductive output in hogfish has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable thermal regime of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. At this temperature, during the peak of the spawning season, females produce a large number of eggs per spawning event, with each female releasing over two thousand eggs per spawning [N_R_i = two thousand eggs per spawning] and spawning occurring every 3 to 5 days [F_R_i = spawning occurring every 3 to 5 days]. This high fecundity observed at this temperature underscores the strong influence of thermal conditions on gametogenesis and spawning behavior in warm-water teleosts. Spawning activity in the wild is synchronized with seasonal temperature cycles, with peak reproductive effort occurring during the late spring and summer months when water temperatures are most favorable for egg and larval development. The substantial daily output allows for considerable larval dispersal potential across the reef habitat, ensuring that a cohort of offspring is released into the plankton over an extended spawning window.

The initial life stage of hogfish begins with the hatching of pelagic eggs that are minute in size. The wet weight at birth for newly emerged yolk-sac larvae is approximately 0.00039 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00039 grams], a remarkably small mass that reflects the tiny egg diameter typical of labrid fishes. This birth weight is based on an estimated egg diameter of 0.9 millimeters, comparable to that observed in related species such as Labrus merula, from which the spherical volume calculation yields the corresponding larval mass. Upon hatching, the endotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves for nutrition, absorbing these nutrients progressively as the mouth and digestive system continue to develop. The yolk-sac stage lasts for several days before the larvae transition to first exogenous feeding, at which point they must successfully capture planktonic prey to sustain further growth. The pelagic larval phase may persist for weeks, during which the tiny drifters disperse widely via ocean currents before metamorphosis and settlement into suitable benthic habitat.

Longevity records for hogfish indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years], based on otolith age validation studies conducted across the species' geographic range at a temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This lifespan estimate was derived from individuals maintained under natural thermal conditions averaging 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], which corresponds to the typical water temperatures encountered throughout their subtropical and tropical distribution. The maximum adult body mass achieved over this extended lifespan can reach 13159 grams [Wwi = 13159 grams], representing the ultimate wet weight attained by the largest males in the population. The relationship between age and body size in hogfish is well described by a power function derived from extensive field sampling, allowing accurate prediction of mass from length across all life stages. This substantial size and extended lifespan are characteristic of large labrids, which tend to grow slowly, mature late, and enjoy relatively low natural mortality rates once they reach adulthood. The combination of a long lifespan and high daily fecundity results in a significant lifetime reproductive output for each successful individual.
